strengths: Introduces a genuinely large-scale, human-annotated dataset of 5,062 LLM-generated proofs across 1,010 problems from prestigious competitions (IMO Shortlist, USAMO, Putnam, EGMO, etc.), which is a significant and costly resource contribution to a field that previously lacked such data.

Rigorous data collection methodology: judges are former IMO participants/qualifiers, a pilot phase was used to refine guidelines, ~10% of proofs were double-graded to estimate inter-annotator agreement (90.4%, implying ~5% individual error rate), and clear written grading guidelines were iteratively developed.

The dataset is thoughtfully structured into purpose-built splits (MathArena, PutnamBench, Best-of-n, Generic) that directly enable answering the three motivating research questions (formal vs. informal, final-answer vs. proof correctness, best-of-n selection).

Provides several novel and well-supported empirical findings: informal proof generation vastly outperforms formal (Lean) methods on PutnamBench, final-answer accuracy is a poor proxy for proof validity (especially for O3), and ranking-based best-of-n strategies meaningfully outperform naive discrete/continuous judging.

Demonstrates practical utility of the dataset by fine-tuning an 8B open model via GRPO that matches Gemini-2.5-Pro's proof-judging accuracy, a compelling proof-of-concept for downstream training value.

Includes useful qualitative failure-mode analysis (inequality sign errors, synthetic geometry mistakes, spurious citation behavior, overgeneralization) that adds interpretive depth beyond aggregate statistics.
Thorough documentation of prompts, grading interface, and methodology in the appendix supports reproducibility of the pipeline (modulo the human annotation cost).
weaknesses: Some key quantitative claims rest on small subsets, e.g., the full pass@n vs. best-of-n comparison with all 8 human-graded generations is based on only 60 problems, limiting statistical confidence in the reported trends.

Only ~10% of the dataset is double-graded for reliability estimation; the single-judge label for the remaining 90% could carry unquantified noise that propagates into benchmarking and training results.

The formal vs. informal proof generation comparison, while informative, pits a formal-proving-specialized model (DeepSeek-Prover-V2) against general-purpose SOTA LLMs (Gemini-2.5-Pro) on a task defined by the informal setup (appended final answer), which may somewhat overstate the raw gap rather than isolating paradigm differences.

The paper's technical/methodological novelty is modest — the core contribution is a dataset and benchmarking exercise rather than a new algorithm or theoretical insight; the best-of-n ranking method is largely adapted from prior work (Liu et al., 2025).

Coverage skews heavily toward high-school-level competitions, with only a small undergraduate slice (Putnam, IMC); this limits claims about model capability at the research or advanced-university level, a limitation the authors acknowledge.

Data contamination risk from public competition problems is acknowledged but not empirically investigated (e.g., no decontamination check or comparison against known training cutoffs), leaving open the possibility that reported 'correct proof' rates are partly inflated by memorization on some subsets.

Self-judging bias analysis (Table 3) is based on relatively few models/proofs and could benefit from more statistical rigor (e.g., confidence intervals) given the paper's own emphasis on rigor elsewhere.

Reproducibility of the human-annotation pipeline itself is inherently limited for the broader community, since replicating comparable expert (ex-IMO) judge panels is costly and not scalable, somewhat undercutting the 'benchmarking pipeline' framing for future work.

strengths: Presents a genuinely large-scale, carefully constructed human-annotated dataset (5,062 proofs, 1,010 problems) using qualified judges (former IMO participants), which addresses a real gap relative to smaller or less open prior efforts.

Methodology for grading is thorough: pilot phase, detailed written guidelines, double-grading for ~10% of data with reported inter-judge agreement (90.4%), abstention/uncertainty options, and a coordinator role for quality control.
The dataset is split into purpose-built subsets (MathArena, PutnamBench, Best-of-n, Generic) that directly support several distinct research questions, which is a thoughtful design choice.

Provides a range of empirical analyses (formal vs. informal proof generation, final-answer vs. proof-correctness gap, best-of-n/ranking strategies, LLM-as-judge capability) that are of practical interest to the community.
Demonstrates one concrete downstream use of the dataset by fine-tuning an 8B judge model that reaches near-parity with GEMINI-2.5-PRO on proof grading, illustrating practical utility.
Includes useful qualitative error analysis (inequality sign errors, synthetic geometry failures, overgeneralization, spurious citations) that adds interpretive value beyond the aggregate numbers.
Open-sourcing of data, interface, and prompts, which benefits reproducibility and downstream community use.
weaknesses: Primary contribution is a dataset and descriptive analysis rather than a new method or theoretical insight; several of the 'key findings' (e.g., final-answer accuracy failing to reflect proof correctness) are confirmatory of concurrent/prior work (Guo et al. 2025b, Petrov et al. 2025, Mahdavi et al. 2025) rather than novel.

The formal vs. informal comparison on PutnamBench is confounded: formal provers are narrowly fine-tuned for Lean and verified automatically under strict formal criteria, while natural-language models are graded under a lenient human rubric (5+/7 threshold); the 11x framing may overstate the generality of the conclusion.

No confidence intervals, error bars, or significance testing accompany the many percentage comparisons throughout the paper (Figs. 3-7, Tables 2-3), despite some comparisons being based on modest sample sizes (e.g., 60 problems for full best-of-n judgments, 114 PutnamBench problems), which weakens the strength of the quantitative claims.

The fine-tuned OPC-R1-8B judge model is evaluated only in-distribution (train/test split from the same generic subset), a limitation the authors themselves note; this substantially undercuts the claimed significance of matching GEMINI-2.5-PRO, since out-of-distribution robustness is untested.

The 'Generic' subset usable for training is relatively small (676 problems), raising concerns about the long-term utility of the dataset for more substantial training efforts beyond judge fine-tuning.

Grading criteria (treating anything scoring 5+/7 as 'correct') introduce a somewhat ad hoc and lenient notion of correctness that may not align with stricter proof-validity standards used elsewhere in the literature, complicating comparison with other benchmarks.
Self-bias analysis (Table 3) and other breakdowns are based on fairly small per-cell counts, limiting the robustness of claims about self-favoring judge behavior.

The problems are overwhelmingly high-school level with limited undergraduate/research-level coverage, restricting the dataset's relevance for studying more advanced mathematical reasoning (acknowledged as a limitation but not mitigated).
Potential data contamination from public competition sources is acknowledged but not empirically investigated or controlled for, despite its direct relevance to the validity of reported accuracies.

The introduction of LLM-generated issue summaries mid-study to aid judges, while checked for aggregate agreement-rate shifts, could still subtly bias the qualitative justifications or annotation consistency in ways not fully explored.

strengths: Introduces a large-scale (5,062 proofs, 1,010 problems), carefully human-annotated dataset filling a clear gap: existing proof-evaluation benchmarks are small, outdated, or not fully open-sourced.

Rigorous annotation methodology: judges are former IMO participants/qualifiers, detailed grading guidelines developed iteratively with a pilot phase, abstention/uncertainty mechanisms, and inter-judge agreement measurement (90.4%) with an estimated per-judge error rate.

The dataset is explicitly designed with distinct splits (MathArena, PutnamBench, Best-of-n, Generic) tailored to answer specific open research questions, demonstrating thoughtful experimental design rather than ad hoc collection.

Produces several genuinely useful empirical findings: a large informal-vs-formal proof generation gap, a substantial final-answer-vs-proof-correctness discrepancy that varies by model, and clear gains from best-of-n/ranking-based selection strategies.
Demonstrates practical downstream utility by fine-tuning an 8B open model via GRPO on the corpus that matches Gemini-2.5-Pro's judging accuracy, showing the dataset's value beyond mere benchmarking.

Includes rich qualitative analysis of failure modes (inequality sign errors, synthetic geometry mistakes, spurious citations, overgeneralization), adding interpretive value beyond aggregate statistics.
Plans to open-source data, interface, and guidelines, which should have meaningful positive impact on the community's ability to train and evaluate proof-generation models.
weaknesses: Only ~10% of proofs are double-graded; the bulk of correctness labels rely on a single annotator, and the paper does not analyze potential systematic differences in strictness/bias across the 13 judges beyond aggregate agreement.

Most results are reported as point-estimate percentages without confidence intervals or significance testing (e.g., Figs. 3-7, Table 2/3), making it hard to assess how robust some comparisons (especially on smaller subsets like the 60-problem best-of-n set) truly are.

The formal-vs-informal proof generation comparison, while interesting, may be confounded by differences in model scale/training focus between general-purpose LLMs and specialized formal provers, and this nuance is underexplored in the discussion.

Dataset is heavily skewed toward high-school-level competition problems, limiting insight into frontier/research-level mathematical reasoning capability (acknowledged as a limitation but not mitigated).
Potential data contamination from public competition problems is acknowledged but not quantified or empirically investigated (e.g., via contamination-detection methods).

The GRPO-finetuned judge model is trained and evaluated on the same distribution (in-domain split), so claims of practical utility/generalization are not verified on out-of-distribution proofs or problems.

Limited detail on annotation logistics (time spent per proof, judge compensation, total annotation cost) reduces reproducibility and makes it harder to gauge scalability of the collection pipeline for future dataset extensions.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely large-scale, carefully human-validated dataset (5,000+ proofs, 1,000+ problems) graded by 13 qualified expert judges (former IMO participants), with a rigorous pipeline including pilot phase, double-grading (~10%), inter-judge agreement analysis, and iteratively refined grading guidelines.

Directly and convincingly addresses three genuinely open and important questions in the field: formal vs. informal proof generation gap, final-answer accuracy vs. proof correctness, and effectiveness of best-of-n selection strategies, providing concrete empirical evidence where prior work only speculated.

Strong practical utility demonstration: fine-tuning an 8B model via GRPO on the dataset yields a judge that is competitive with GPT-5/Gemini-2.5-Pro at a fraction of the cost, and the improvement is shown to partially generalize to out-of-distribution (undergraduate-level) data.
Thorough attention to reproducibility and transparency: open dataset, code, detailed prompts, and reproducibility statement; careful discussion and empirical checks of data contamination effects.

Rich complementary analyses (self-evaluation bias of LLM judges, qualitative error taxonomy such as overgeneralization/citation hallucination, category/difficulty breakdowns) that add depth beyond the headline results.
Novel and interesting best-of-n ranking method (Swiss-system Bradley-Terry ranking) that shows non-trivial gains and scaling behavior over standard discrete/continuous selection.
weaknesses: The dataset skews heavily toward high-school level competitions (~84%), limiting insight into research-level or more advanced mathematical reasoning, and only a small undergraduate subset (Putnam) is available for that regime.

Several key comparisons rely on fairly small subsets (e.g., 60 problems for the exhaustive best-of-n analysis, 114 problems for PutnamBench, 152 for best-of-n overall), yielding wide confidence intervals that sometimes overlap substantially between models/methods despite the paper's narrative framing certain differences as clear or significant.

The formal vs. informal proof generation comparison, while informative, is not fully controlled: informal models benefit from being general-purpose frontier systems while the formal baseline is a specialized (and non-agentic) prover; the paper acknowledges this but the headline '4x' framing may overstate a clean apples-to-apples comparison.

The claim that LLMs are 'human-level' proof judges rests on a single dataset/setting (binary correctness with curated prompts) and contrasts with prior work (Petrov et al.) partly by design differences (binary vs. continuous scoring); broader validation across settings/scales of proofs would strengthen this claim.

A bug affecting 18 questions in the Rank (Swiss) evaluation was discovered and those items excluded post-hoc, which, combined with the already limited sample size, raises some concern about the robustness of the best-of-n results.

LLM-generated 'issue summaries' were shown to graders as an aid before their final judgment; although the authors report no measurable agreement shift, potential subtle anchoring bias from this design choice cannot be fully ruled out.

The contribution is primarily a resource/benchmark paper with an accompanying empirical study rather than a new algorithmic or theoretical method, and some findings (e.g., final-answer/proof-correctness gap) mainly confirm prior smaller-scale observations rather than being fully novel.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely large and carefully constructed human-annotated dataset (5,062 proofs, 1,010 problems) graded by 13 qualified expert judges (former IMO participants), with a documented pilot phase, inter-judge agreement measurement (~90.4%), and iterative refinement of grading guidelines.

Tackles three concretely important and under-studied questions in the field (formal vs. informal proof generation gap, final-answer accuracy vs. proof correctness, and best-of-n selection for proof quality) rather than just releasing a static benchmark.

Provides substantial transparency: detailed grading instructions, prompts, contamination analysis, out-of-distribution evaluation of the fine-tuned judge model, and qualitative failure-mode analysis (inequality sign errors, geometry angle mistakes, spurious citations, overgeneralization).

Dataset and pipeline appear reproducible, with code, dataset, guidelines, and interface documentation included; problems span a wide range of well-known competitions with metadata on difficulty and source.
Demonstrates a concrete downstream use case (fine-tuning an 8B judge model) that meaningfully improves over its base model, illustrating the dataset's practical utility.
weaknesses: Several headline claims rest on small subsets with wide confidence intervals (e.g., best-of-n results on only 60/134 problems, formal-vs-informal PutnamBench comparison on 114 problems), yet are stated with strong rhetorical confidence (e.g., '4x more problems', '17% improvement') without adequately caveating the uncertainty.

A bug in the Rank (Swiss) method invalidated results for 18 questions, which were simply excluded post hoc — this raises concerns about the overall care taken in the experimental pipeline and whether other undetected issues exist.

The problem-selection process was adaptively tuned during data collection to target ~50% model accuracy, which risks selection bias and complicates interpretation of aggregate 'proof correctness' statistics as representative of general model capability.

The 'LLM issue summaries' shown to human judges during grading were validated for bias only via a coarse before/after agreement-rate check with a single model (O4-mini judge), which is a fairly weak test for a design choice that could subtly anchor human judgments.

The formal-vs-informal proof generation comparison is somewhat apples-to-oranges: informal proof correctness is assessed via the same imperfect human/LLM grading pipeline (with an estimated ~5-10% error rate), whereas formal proofs are verified by a proof checker with no such noise, potentially inflating the perceived informal-formal gap.

The paper bundles many loosely related analyses (proof generation, formal/informal gap, final-answer/proof gap, best-of-n, LLM-as-judge, fine-tuning) into a single submission, which dilutes depth of investigation in each individual area and results in somewhat shallow treatment of confounds for each specific claim.

The dataset skews heavily toward high-school-level competition problems (~84%), limiting the generalizability of findings to more advanced or research-level mathematical reasoning, which is acknowledged but not substantially mitigated.

The 'LLMs are human-level judges' framing is based on comparing single-model pass@1 against a double-graded agreement rate computed over a different (broader) set of proofs than the actual test set, making the 'human baseline' comparison somewhat indirect rather than a matched, apples-to-apples evaluation.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely large-scale, high-quality resource (5,000+ proofs, 1,000+ problems) graded by 13 IMO-caliber human judges, filling a clear gap in the literature relative to prior small/private/non-open efforts (Petrov et al., Mahdavi et al., Guo et al.).

Rigorous data-collection methodology: careful judge selection, detailed grading guidelines developed iteratively via a pilot phase, double-grading (~10%) with quantified inter-judge agreement (90.4%, implied 5% per-judge error rate), and use of LLM-generated issue summaries whose lack of bias was empirically verified.

The dataset design directly targets and convincingly answers three well-motivated open questions: (1) natural language vs. formal proof generation gap (4x difference on PutnamBench), (2) final-answer accuracy vs. proof correctness misalignment (e.g., O3's ~30% drop), and (3) effectiveness of best-of-n/ranking selection strategies, with the Swiss/Bradley-Terry ranking method showing clear and interesting scaling behavior beyond simple discrete/continuous approaches.

Practical demonstration of dataset utility via GRPO fine-tuning of an 8B model that approaches frontier proprietary models (GPT-5, Grok-4) on proof judging, including an OOD generalization check (undergraduate Putnam problems) and self-bias/self-evaluation analysis.
Thorough contamination analysis using multiple angles (standard vs. non-standard competitions, providing ground-truth solutions to judges) that meaningfully strengthens confidence in the results.

Strong transparency and reproducibility: detailed prompts, grading interface documentation, guidelines, and dataset splits designed explicitly for downstream training/evaluation use; qualitative error analysis (inequality sign errors, synthetic geometry failures, spurious citations, overgeneralization) adds valuable insight beyond aggregate numbers.
weaknesses: Some key sub-analyses rely on quite small subsets (e.g., 60 problems for the full pass@n vs. best-of-n comparison, 134 for the larger best-of-n subset), leading to wide confidence intervals; the paper acknowledges this but conclusions about ranking-method superiority would benefit from more data.
Most proofs (~90%) are graded by only a single judge, so the reported 5% per-judge error rate is an extrapolation from a subset rather than a dataset-wide guarantee of label quality.
The dataset skews heavily toward high-school-level competitions (~84%), limiting insight into more advanced/research-level mathematical reasoning, an explicitly acknowledged limitation.
A methodological bug in the Rank (Swiss) best-of-n experiment caused 18 questions to be excluded post hoc, which slightly undercuts confidence in that specific result's precision.
Self-evaluation/self-bias analysis is limited to only four models with proofs from all four available, restricting generality of the finding that models judge their own proofs worse.

Despite the contamination mitigation experiments, the paper concedes the Gemini-2.5-Pro vs. O4-mini gap in §5.1 cannot be conclusively attributed to genuine capability differences rather than contamination, slightly weakening one of the reported findings.

GPT-5 and Grok-4 were not evaluated as proof generators (only as judges) since they were released after data collection, leaving the top-line proof-generation leaderboard slightly dated relative to current frontier models.
